defect:A4-counter-valve-severity-mismatc.title: The blocker counter and its release valve disagree about severity, and a run cannot converge because of it
defect:A4-counter-valve-severity-mismatc.what: `unverified_critical_count()` counts findings with **no severity test at all** — it skips non-UNCONFIRMED, already-escalated and exhausted entries, then counts whatever is left. But the only thing that can RELEASE an entry from that count, the `exhausted` valve, requires severity of 0.7 or above. So a sub-critical finding can ENTER the tally of findings that block convergence, and has no way out of it.
defect:A4-counter-valve-severity-mismatc.why: It is live and it blocked a real run. Finding C0042 in `study_run1b_2026-10-03` sits at severity 0.6 with a zero-character falsifier, emitted in round 2 and never given one. Leave-one-out on the live registry: removing it drops the blocker count from 1 to 0. It blocks the zero-critical streak for every remaining round, so **that run could not converge**. You issued `d` on 2026-10-03 and nothing has changed since, so the run is still obstructed.
options: **Make the counter and the valve share ONE severity predicate** — the symmetric fix, and the one the defect record itself asks for. A finding either enters the blocker tally and can be released from it, or it does neither.

**Restore the severity gate to the counter**, so only criticals ever enter it. Measured consequence: that takes the blocker tally from 3 to 0 on this run's pre-sweep registry, after which the gate blocks on `contested=2` and the zero-critical streak instead.
**Lower the valve's severity requirement** to match the counter, which releases sub-criticals but weakens what `exhausted` means.
defect:A4-counter-valve-severity-mismatc.evidence_line: The counter's own docstring claims it counts `severity >= CRITICAL_SEVERITY_THRESHOLD`, which its body does not do — stale since the gate was removed on 2026-09-06. A second defect found alongside: `exhausted_round_threshold` defaulted to 8 while the maximum reachable age in an 8-round run is 7, so the valve could not fire in ANY 8-round run; z3 returns unsat, NumPy's enumeration of all 36 legal pairs gives max age 7, SymPy gives the general condition T <= R-1. defect:integrity-gate-interpreter-carve-.title: The integrity gate refuses a correct falsifier, and must refuse it by construction
defect:integrity-gate-interpreter-carve-.what: The sandbox integrity gate allows the harness's own Python 3.13 directories. A falsifier that spawns a second interpreter gets macOS's own Python 3.9 at `/usr/bin/python3`, whose standard library sits under `/Library` and whose user-site sits under `~` — both inside the denied regions. Its ordinary import reads are recorded as denials, and **any** denial becomes an INTEGRITY_VIOLATION.
defect:integrity-gate-interpreter-carve-.why: It is structural, not incidental. Finding C0050's falsifier spawns `/usr/bin/python3` precisely BECAUSE the defect it demonstrates is that the target prescribes a bare unpinned `python3`. Any falsifier for that defect class must do the same thing, so the gate is guaranteed to refuse the correct falsifier. C0050 is severity 0.7 — a critical — and was recorded as untested and pushed to a human. Proved by counterfactual: with the 3.9 roots allowed, the identical falsifier returns CONFIRMED instead of INTEGRITY_VIOLATION.
options: **Run it and flag the denials as a reporting metric** rather than refusing. This is the option the defect record leans toward, and it has a measured side effect worth knowing: the finding stops being `contested`, which removes a second obstruction to convergence on its own.
**Keep refusing and widen the carve-out** to include system interpreters. This preserves the refusal but means `contested` must be named explicitly in the fix, or the convergence bug survives it.
**Keep refusing with no change**, accepting that this defect class can never be falsified inside the harness.
defect:integrity-gate-interpreter-carve-.evidence_line: The refuse-rather-than-flag behaviour entered on 2026-08-15 in a milestone merge citing NO founder ruling, and you confirmed on 2026-10-03 that you were never consulted. Cost on this run: 34 matched-read lines and 6 banners over-reported for one finding.

task:B77.title: B77 — whether to adopt the roster-aware convergence window, which requires a run missing seats to stay quiet for proportionally longer before it may close
task:B77.spoken_heading: WHETHER THE CONVERGENCE GATE SHOULD KNOW HOW MANY SEATS ARE ANSWERING
task:B77.what: The live convergence check takes 10 parameters and not 1 of them names the roster. That matters because 1 of its 2 sides counts consecutive rounds in which no new critical finding arrived, and that count gets easier to satisfy as the roster shrinks: fewer seats generate fewer findings, and the gate cannot tell a quiet healthy panel from a quiet depleted panel. An unadopted seat design written on 2026-10-07 repairs it by scaling the requirement, so a run missing seats has to stay quiet for proportionally longer before it may close. Its reasoning was checked rather than taken on trust, in 4 steps: the bound never asks for less than the exact requirement at any level of correlation between seats, 0 violations over 12,000 combinations, and it is exact rather than merely safe when seats are independent. 1 precondition the design does not state was found during that check, and is recorded with it: a panel whose critical rate is 0 gives an undefined requirement, and the design covers only the case of an empty roster. The case it addresses is real rather than hypothetical. 3 of 53 archived runs carry a round in which fewer seats answered than were taking part, and 1 of those is the failure of 18 July that the runner's own code describes in a comment. A SECOND REPAIR FOR THE SAME DEFECT WAS FOUND ON 2026-11-02 AND IT IS THE DESIGN NOW RECOMMENDED. A different seat, writing to the same brief on 2026-10-07, repaired it by counting quiet SEAT-ROUNDS rather than quiet rounds: the requirement becomes the roster size times the round count, and each round contributes however many seats actually answered. At a full roster, and at any roster that stays the same size, the 2 rules are literally the same rule, confirmed symbolically and over every roster size from 1 to 6 with 0 disagreements. They come apart when the roster CHANGES between rounds, which is the only shape the archive actually holds: all 3 degraded runs have a single short round with full rounds on at least 1 side. The first rule takes a single number for how many seats are live, so a run whose roster changed has to be given 1 value and the rule does not say which, and the 2 sensible choices disagree by as much as 6 rounds. On a run that lost 4 of 6 seats for 1 round and recovered, the second rule asks for 5 quiet rounds, while the first asks for 9 if you take the worst round and 3 if you take the last. The second rule has no such choice to make. It also aims at a bigger target: the stricter of the 2 convergence gates, which is the gate in force, has a fallback path where closing rests on the quiet count alone, and that gate takes 3 inputs of which none names the roster. A THIRD DESIGN WAS FOUND ON 2026-11-02 AND IT IS THE DESIGN NOW RECOMMENDED, which means this recommendation has changed twice. The same seat that wrote the first design also wrote a second design in the same brief, and that second design is the more complete. The 3 are not 3 rival answers once seen side by side. The first states the exact requirement and then takes a safe upper bound on it, which is why it needs no measured inputs. The third computes that same exact requirement, which costs it a dependence on 2 measured numbers. The second, from the other seat, restates the upper bound in a form that stays defined when the roster changes between rounds. The bound is never too small, checked over 36 combinations of roster size and correlation, and it is substantially looser: at a 1-seat roster it demands 18 quiet rounds where the exact requirement is 9 to 11, and at 2 seats 9 against 6 to 7. Every extra round is an extra round of every seat's time, and on a paid roster it is paid. WHAT DECIDES IT IS THAT THE THIRD DESIGN'S CASE FOR COMBINING ITS 2 PARTS IS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSERTED, and it is the only such case found all day. Its own committed falsifier runs clean and shows each part curing a failure the other cannot: with only the record of who answered, the run is labelled degraded but still closes too early, at 2.4796 times its full-roster risk; with only the raised requirement, the risk is held but a reader sees the same record as a full-roster run; with both, it closes properly, is labelled degraded, and sits at 0.7125 of target. A healthy run pays nothing, and a run with no live seats does not converge at all. It also covers the gap the first design leaves, where a panel that never raises a critical finding gives an undefined requirement.
task:B77.why: Yours because adopting it changes how a pre-registered convergence threshold is computed, and the standing directive on the decay curve reserves that surface to you. It also sits beside B76, where you already have the question of whether the 2 enabled convergence criteria may disagree, so the gate now carries 2 questions rather than 1. Nothing has been wired either way.
options: **Adopt the exact version**, which is my recommendation on the simplest sufficient and additive standards. It is 1 file, it holds the risk at or below the full-roster value at every roster size from 1 to 6, it costs a healthy run nothing, and its case for combining its 2 parts is the only measured one in this arc. Its reasoning is cross-checked 2 ways inside the design, agreeing with an independent numerical calculation to better than 1 part in 1,000,000,000, and a constraint solver confirms its 2 labels cannot both apply and that the quiet count alone cannot tell the 2 causes apart.

**Adopt the safe upper bound instead**, in the seat-rounds form, if you would rather not depend on 2 measured numbers at all. It is never too small and it stays defined when the roster changes between rounds, at the cost of up to 9 extra quiet rounds at a very small roster.

**Leave it unadopted** and accept that a run losing seats may close sooner than its pre-registered threshold intended. The status quo, and not neutral: at 2 live seats the chance of a falsely quiet window is 2.4796 times the full-roster value, and the gate cannot see the difference.

The degraded-round rate is 3 of 53 runs, 0.056604, with a 95 percent interval from 0.019437 to 0.153702. The 2 repairs were shown identical at a constant roster symbolically and by enumeration, and divergent on a varying one by worked example. My first attempt to measure the degraded rate returned 0 of 0 and that was the instrument rather than the answer. task:B81.title: B81 — the commit gate costs more than the limit written in its own header
task:B81.what: Every commit runs a set of fast correctness tests first and refuses the commit if any are red. That set's own header states its design limit in these words: *"A per-commit gate costing 11 minutes would be bypassed within a day, and a guard that gets bypassed is not a guard."* 11 minutes is 660 seconds. Measured across this session's 4 commits the gate took 800, 769, 738 and 745 seconds — 4 of 4 above the limit, mean 763.00, standard deviation 28.011902, and a one-sided t-test against 660 gives t = 7.354017 and p = 0.002598, agreed by SciPy and by an mpmath integration of the t density to 6 decimal places.
task:B81.why: The cause is structural rather than careless and the header says so itself: 1 of the guards is parametrised per completed task entry, so the gate's cost GROWS WITH THE TASK LIST. It is not a fixed price. The header's own measurement of 277 tests in a median 7.09 seconds was taken when the guard list held 7 files; it now holds about 125. What is missing is not the measurement, which exists and is accurate — exactly 2 files read the recorded duration, the hook that writes it and `sv` which consumes it, and nothing compares it against the limit. So the project has written down a standard, measured itself exceeding it, and has nothing that would ever say so.
options: **Add a guard that fails when the gate exceeds its own stated limit, and split the set into a commit-time tier and a periodic tier.** This is the recommendation. Simplest sufficient: the guard needs no new figure, because both numbers already exist in files; the same change should have the hook APPEND each duration to a committed ledger rather than overwrite 1 number, so the series becomes verifiable by any later session. Additive: no guard is removed and no test is dropped; what is added is a loud signal that the set has outgrown its tier. Note that it would start refusing commits immediately, which is the point — the split becomes deliberate rather than silent.

**Build the reachedness guard's body index once instead of per script name, and only then decide on tiers.** Measured: that guard scans 10,705 file bodies totalling 482.02 MiB for each of 572 script names, which bounds the work at 6,123,260 name-by-body pairs and 269.25 GiB of string search -- a BOUND rather than the work, because the loop breaks on the first body that mentions a script, so the realised cost is on the order of half that; it consumed over 4 minutes of CPU on its own against 51.54 seconds for an 8-file set without it. Indexing once turns that into a single pass. **NOT recommended without evidence first**: it changes a RATCHET, so its 2 verdict sets must be compared element-by-element before it is applied, because an optimisation that silently drops a match loosens the ratchet by the width of what it dropped.

**Raise the written limit to match the measurement.** Honest bookkeeping, but it concedes the header's own argument that a gate this expensive gets bypassed, and it would need raising again the next time the task list grows.
**Leave it.** The cost is real but bounded, and `sv` already derives its timeout from the measurement so the save path is protected. What this accepts is that the stated standard is decorative.

**Decide which files the gate should watch, not only how long it may take.** Cost and coverage trade directly: the gate costs 745 s and watches 120 of 785 test files. Tonight a 21-test guard on the tool that decides whether work stops was found red after 5 commits, because it is 1 of the 665 the gate does not run. Adding files raises the cost the first option would cap, so the 2 halves are one decision.
task:B81.evidence_line: 4 of 4 commits this session exceeded 660 s at 800, 769, 738 and 745 seconds, Wilson 95% [0.510109, 1.000000], Clopper-Pearson [0.397635, 1.000000]; n = 4 from 1 session on 1 machine, so this establishes the limit is exceeded here and not a population rate. The 4 durations were read serially from a scratch file that keeps only the last, so the series is not recomputable from the repository; making it so is part of what this asks for. The dominant cost is not the guard the header blames: test_scripts_are_reached scans the whole tracked tree, 11,116 files and 482.02 MiB, once per script name. And the gate watches 120 of 785 test files, 15.2866%, Wilson [0.129388, 0.179726]: a 21-test guard on the triage tool sat outside it and was red for 5 commits before being run by hand.

task:B88.title: B88 - the fold-back gate now accepts, which exposes whether its suite can see the target at all

task:B88.what: `_apply_back_gate` required a clean exit from a suite it ran in a sandbox that excludes `bench/logs`, so a suite reading the archive failed there whatever the candidate said. 19 findings in 1 run were refused with the identical reason, and across the archive the facility had promoted 0 of 34. The exposure is measured rather than theoretical: 7 of 7 prose runs in the archive were handed a suite chosen by argparse rather than for the target, the earliest on 2026-10-03.

ADDITIVE: nothing is removed, and the gate is still available to any run that names its own suite. It leaves 1 residual, stated plainly: a Python target given a wrong but EXPLICIT suite is still unprotected.
